extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners / Office personnel (and patent practitioners evaluating obviousness)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a claimed invention is obvious under §103 using an 'obvious to try' rationale and related obviousness doctrines (predictability, motivation to combine, common sense, cross-field adaptations). Intended to direct factual findings and reasoning examiners must make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious To Try — Four Required Findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on an 'obvious to try' rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and then articulate: (1) a finding that at the time of the invention there had been a recognized problem or need in the art; (2) a finding that there had been a finite number of identified, predictable potential solutions to the recognized need or problem; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have pursued the known potential solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any of these findings cannot be made, the 'obvious to try' rationale cannot be used to support a conclusion of obviousness. Examiners must explicitly state these findings in the record and tie them to the Graham factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual Factors for Obvious To Try (predictability focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: An obvious-to-try inquiry must be undertaken in the context of the subject matter in question, including the characteristics of the science or technology, its state of advance, the nature of the known choices, the specificity or generality of the prior art, and the predictability of results in the area of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should evaluate predictability and reasonable expectations of success in view of the technology's characteristics and case law (e.g., Abbott Labs.). Chemical arts often receive particular attention for predictability issues. Provide factual support showing how these contextual factors affect predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite Number of Identified, Predictable Solutions (what 'finite' means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is a design need or market pressure and there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, a person of ordinary skill has good reason to pursue known options; in such circumstances, 'obvious to try' may show obviousness. 'Finite' in context means a number that is 'small or easily traversed' in the context of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document prior art that narrows the field to a limited set of options (Pfizer: 53 pharmaceutically acceptable salts as an example). Show that the set is small/easily traversed for someone skilled in the art (Takeda/Ortho-McNeil distinction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Expectation of Success
rubrics_metrics.description: One of ordinary skill in the art must have been able to pursue the known potential solutions with a reasonable expectation of success for an 'obvious to try' rejection to be proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of reasonable expectation can include prior art teaching that a variable is result-effective or routine methods that would predictably produce the claimed result (e.g., Kubin: conventional methods would have given reasonable expectation of obtaining the nucleic acid). Lack of absolute predictability does not preclude reasonable expectation if the art suggests success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious To Try Not Appropriate When Prior Art Offers Only Vague Guidance or Numerous Undirected Options
rubrics_metrics.description: An obvious-to-try rationale is erroneous when (1) it would have been 'obvious to try' merely to vary all parameters or try many possible choices where the prior art gives no indication which parameters are critical or which choices are likely to succeed, or (2) it would have been to explore a new technology or general approach where the prior art gives only general guidance as to the particular form of the claimed invention or how to achieve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this limitation when prior art leaves too many undirected options or only general exploratory guidance; cite Kubin and O'Farrell reasoning. If prior art does not indicate which parameters or choices are promising, do not rely on 'obvious to try.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching Away and Motivation to Combine
rubrics_metrics.description: If the primary reference contains no express teaching away from the proposed modification and the prior art identifies result-effective variables, this supports a motivation to combine references and may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record whether prior art suggests modification, identifies variables (e.g., reaction time, degree of hydrolysis), and lacks teaching away (Urbanski example). Show how prior art would have motivated a skilled artisan to modify a base system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common Sense May Inform Obviousness if Reasoned and Supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense can inform the analysis of obviousness if explained with sufficient reasoning and supported by evidence of record; a person of ordinary skill is 'a person of ordinary creativity, not an automaton.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make conclusory appeals to common sense. Provide a reasoned explanation and factual foundation (cases: Perfect Web, Bozek, Zurko). Avoid invoking 'good common sense' without record support; Arendi shows Board must provide reasoned analysis supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected Results or Serendipity Can Defeat Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected results, e.g., unpredicted therapeutic advantages or lack of expected toxicity, can overcome a prima facie case of obviousness and show that the invention was not obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document experimental/clinical evidence of unexpected properties (Sanofi, Ortho-McNeil). Show that outcome was not reasonably predictable and that the inventor would not have had a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art That Narrows a Large Field to a Smaller, Appropriate Set of Options
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere existence of a large number of options does not preclude obviousness when the prior art teachings lead one of ordinary skill to a narrower set of options; that reduced set is the appropriate one to consider for an obvious-to-try inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how prior art funnels choices to a smaller, predictable set (Bayer example). Explain why the narrowed set is the relevant universe of options for the skilled artisan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known Work in One Field Prompting Variations in Another (design incentives/market forces)
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on adaptation of known work from one field to another, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate: (1) that the prior art included a similar or analogous device (method or product); (2) that there were design incentives or market forces prompting adaptation of the known device; and (3) that the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art were encompassed in known variations or in a principle known in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit factual findings tying prior-art analogies, market/design incentives, and known variations to the claimed differences. This rationale requires showing predictable adaptation across fields based on incentives and known principles.
